title: Pick, Pack, Ship: Warehouse Management and Fulfillment
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/15-warehouse-and-fulfillment/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Modalities, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter, plus a roadmap paragraph in the introduction and a synthesis paragraph at the head of the conclusion, which the published page lacked. It is a contract, not a description: places where the chapter did not yet do what the spec asks are listed under open_questions or in the decision log.

know: The warehouse steps (receiving, put-away, slotting, wave or continuous release, picking, packing, shipping confirmation, cycle counting) and what each changes; where automation and robots sit beneath the warehouse system.

The fulfillment order and its lifecycle (requested, accepted or rejected, in progress, shipped, closed incomplete, with cancellation as a request), the warehouse's four interfaces, and the four ways to get warehouse execution (ERP module, dedicated WMS, 3PL, marketplace fulfillment program).
Why the SSCC label and the despatch advice (DESADV) are generated from pack confirmation.
believe: The warehouse system is the only writer of on-hand stock; every other system derives from its events.
Whether an order ships on time depends on when it reaches the warehouse and on the cut-off and backlog, not only on how fast people pick.
can_do: Specify the platform-to-WMS integration: what the fulfillment order carries, its key, the accept-or-reject answer, cancellation after acceptance, shipment confirmations, stock events and the reconciliation behind them.
Say which warehouse facts (cut-off, capacity, backlog) the delivery promise must read.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a peak evening on which orders reached an adequately staffed warehouse hours late, the reader places the fault in the order feed and the promise, not in the warehouse, and names the four remedies.
acceptance_criteria.probe: On a peak evening the warehouse had staff to spare, but orders placed at 20:00 reached the warehouse system after midnight while the storefront kept promising next-day delivery for orders before 22:00. Using only this chapter: where was the fault, and what would have prevented it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: In the order feed into the warehouse system, which created orders one at a time with several calls each and was throttled by the vendor's rate limit, and in a promise that did not read the queue; the warehouse was never the limit. A queue allowed to grow without failing checkout, order creation in batches within the rate limit, a monitor on the age of the oldest unprocessed order, and a cut-off that moves when that age grows. Not a faster warehouse or more pickers.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a duplicated instruction and a late cancellation, the reader says what the fulfillment-order contract does in each case.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A timeout makes the integration send the same order to the warehouse twice; the next morning support cancels another order in the shop after the warehouse had already accepted it. Using only this chapter: what should happen in each case?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The fulfillment order carries an identity (an idempotency key), so the warehouse system recognizes the repeat and reuses the existing instruction: no second pick list, no second jacket. After acceptance a cancellation is a request that the warehouse answers; if picking has started it is rejected, the order stays in progress, support tells the customer, and the item comes back as a return.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say which system must generate the pallet label and the despatch advice for a retail customer, and from what.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A retail customer deducts money because the pallet labels do not match the despatch advice it received. Using only this chapter: which system should generate the SSCC label and the DESADV, and from what?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The warehouse system, at pack time, from what was actually packed (the pack confirmation), never from the order or the ERP's view of it; Kestrel & Pine's W6 moves both there after the €14,200 ASN Chargeback.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why a missing unit or a late instruction becomes a delivery problem; what a warehouse system does from picking to shipping, and where automation and robots fit; the fulfillment order the warehouse receives and its acceptance step; the warehouse as owner of the physical stock count; cut-off, capacity and work release as inputs to the delivery promise; Eva's order at Duiven on 14 April. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's Duiven warehouse and vendor documentation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture; most of all the engineer or architect who must integrate a shop platform, an OMS or a 3PL with a warehouse system (Noor Visser and Ruben Alves at Kestrel & Pine); operations leaders who need to see why 'send the order to the WMS' is not a specification come next (Daniel Okafor).
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side; roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.
Kestrel & Pine, its people, its 2026 and January 2027 incidents in outline and the names of the sixteen failure patterns.

From Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines (money, goods, returns), 'system', 'the shop platform' for the hosted product and 'commerce platform' for the whole set of systems, business models and the four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group), the capability map, bounded context, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation, the Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and order management system, availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.
From Part II: one owner per product attribute, SKU and GTIN, available-to-promise (on hand minus committed minus allocations), one writer each for on hand and committed, per-channel buffers.

From Part III: checkout creating the order once with payment pending; one order record with three status lines and an OMS once two of four conditions hold; the fulfillment order named as the order record's instruction to the warehouse; one invoice per shipment.
From the Part IV introduction: the system on the spot witnesses each physical fact; Eva's jacket was promised for Wednesday and delivered on Thursday; the Queue That Waited in outline.
does_not_know: Warehouse steps: location, put-away, slotting, wave, cluster and batch picking, cartonization, shipping confirmation, cycle counting.
Automation: autonomous mobile robot, goods-to-person, robotic picking, sortation, warehouse execution system, warehouse control system, robot fleet management.
The fulfillment order's lifecycle and its accept-or-reject and cancellation-request handshake.
Cut-off, capacity and release policy as the warehouse's day.
Marketplace fulfillment programs and a stock location the merchant can see but not count.

thesis.question: What happens to an order inside the warehouse, and what must the warehouse system receive from, and report to, the rest of the platform?
thesis.claim: Inside the warehouse an order becomes work that is released, picked, packed and confirmed as a shipment within the building's capacity and before the carrier's collection. The warehouse system must receive a fulfillment order it can accept or reject, carrying only what to ship and a key, so that a retried request creates no second pick list. As the only writer of on-hand stock, it must report shipment confirmations built from what was packed, every stock change as an event, and its cut-off, capacity and backlog.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that 'send the order to the WMS' is the whole specification: the warehouse receives the order as the shop holds it, any system may correct stock figures, and on-time dispatch is a matter of warehouse staffing and speed.
thesis.so_what: On Black Friday 2026 Duiven had the staff, but orders took four hours to reach its warehouse system and roughly 8,000 orders placed between 17:00 and midnight missed next-day delivery while the storefront promised it; the remedy was a queue, batches, a monitor on the oldest order and a moving cut-off, not a faster warehouse. Bergzicht deducted €14,200 because the despatch advice was built from the ERP's order rather than from what was packed. A merchant that accepts the claim writes the fulfillment-order contract, names the one writer of on-hand stock and feeds the cut-off to the promise before it buys a WMS, a 3PL or robots.
thesis.how_why: Physical work cannot be undone by changing a status: once the warehouse has accepted an instruction, picking may have started, so a cancellation needs the warehouse's answer. Prices, payments and customer history change for reasons the warehouse cannot act on and add data it must protect, so the instruction carries only what to ship. A request retried after a timeout arrives twice and, without a key, creates a second pick list. Only the warehouse counts shelves, so any second writer of on-hand stock produces phantom stock. An order that reaches the warehouse after the last wave ships the next day whatever the page said, so the promise must read the cut-off and the backlog. A pallet's SSCC and contents exist only at pack time, so the despatch advice must come from pack confirmation.

supporting_claims.claim: Inside the warehouse an order becomes work that is released in waves or continuously, picked, packed and confirmed as a shipment within the building's capacity and before the carrier's collection; automation changes how the work is executed, not the need to confirm its physical results.

The warehouse system must receive a fulfillment order it accepts or rejects, carrying only what to ship and an identity, so that a retried request creates no second pick list and a cancellation after acceptance is a request the warehouse answers.
The warehouse system is the only writer of on-hand stock and reports every change as an event, with a daily snapshot and a reconciliation to catch what is lost.
What the warehouse reports about a shipment must be built from what was packed: the shipment confirmation per parcel, and for wholesale the SSCC label and the despatch advice generated at pack time.
Whether an order ships on time depends on when it reaches the warehouse and on the cut-off, capacity and backlog, so the delivery promise must read those facts, not a static sentence.

Whoever runs the warehouse software (an ERP module, a dedicated WMS, a 3PL or a marketplace program) changes the operator, not the contract, and the integration must keep pace with the operation's complexity.

role.contribution: Gives the part its warehouse side: the fulfillment order as the contract between the order record and the warehouse, the warehouse system as the only writer of on-hand stock, and the cut-off, capacity and backlog that every later promise must read.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene, then in-practice: the Black Friday queue posed at Duiven and resolved once the contract is known

flow.rationale: The Duiven scene comes first so that every term arrives as part of the answer to Noor's question about the Black Friday queue. What a WMS does comes next because the steps and the three facts of warehouse work (release policy, capacity, physical facts) are what every later section uses. The interfaces follow: the fulfillment order before stock because stock events and confirmations are results of the instruction, the warehouse's day after stock because the promise needs both, and wholesale last because it applies the confirmation rule to pallets. The four execution choices come after the contract because each is a different operator behind the same contract, and the stages after the choices because they say how the setup and its warning signs change as the merchant grows; both come before the worked cases because the cases show Kestrel & Pine at stage 3 with a stage-1 connection, which the stage table names. Automation follows the stages, whose Group row adds it, because it repeats the contract one level down (task identity, confirmed outcome, capacity fed to the promise) and is hypothetical for Duiven; placed before the contract it relied on the fulfillment order and the promise before either was explained (two flow-rubric runs), and placed between the contract and the choices it interrupted the move from what the warehouse exchanges to who runs it (both round-3 flow readers). The worked cases come after the contract and the choices so that Eva's late parcel and the Black Friday queue can be read against the cut-off and the order feed, and the failures come last because each is read against the part of the contract that prevents it. Moving the interfaces before the steps would introduce confirmations and stock events before the reader knows the work that produces them; moving the worked cases before the capacity facts would leave Eva's late parcel unexplained.

hook.content: A picker walks to the shelf for a paid order and finds no jacket. The storefront has already confirmed the sale, but the warehouse now needs to investigate, find a replacement unit or report a failed pick, and those steps may push the parcel past its dispatch cut-off: a stock error has become a delivery problem.

bridge.from_reader_world: Anyone who has had a parcel arrive a day late, or the wrong size in a box, has met a promise the warehouse could not keep; the Part IV introduction has just left Eva's paid order waiting for Duiven.
bridge.to_topic: Whether the warehouse can keep a promise depends on the instruction it receives and the facts it reports, so the question is what those must be.

sections.heading: What a Warehouse Management System Does
sections.controlling_idea: A WMS directs the warehouse's steps and records their results, and three facts about that work (a release policy, finite capacity and physical facts only the WMS sees) shape every integration with it.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the work an order becomes and the three facts the later contract, stock and promise sections rest on.

flow.rationale: The steps first, then how picking is organized, then how products differ, then the three facts generalized from the work: the facts are drawn from the steps, so they cannot come first.

transition_in.introduces: What the warehouse system does, step by step.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A WMS directs warehouse work and records its results, and each of its steps, from receiving to cycle counting, changes what the building holds or what can ship.

evidence.what: Eight steps (receiving, put-away, slotting, wave or batch release, picking, packing and cartonization, shipping confirmation, cycle counting), each with a plain definition and what it changes.
evidence.shows: Each step changes stock or what ships today; the shipping confirmation is the step that fulfils the order and reduces on hand.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Picking methods organize the pickers' travel differently, by collecting several orders in one trip (cluster picking) or their items together for separation at packing (batch picking), as Odoo and Picqer document, while larger products such as Manhattan's also release different order types together.

evidence.what: Odoo (waves, cluster and batch picking), Picqer (batch pick lists and routes), Manhattan's Order Streaming (n.d., accessed November 2026).
evidence.shows: The grouping methods are documented product features, not Kestrel & Pine's invention.

transition_in.introduces: How picking routes are organized.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: WMS products also serve buildings of different complexity, from basic location tracking to highly automated warehouses, and Duiven uses locations, waves and scanning with no automation.

evidence.what: Infios, formerly Körber Supply Chain Software, complexity levels (n.d., accessed November 2026).
evidence.shows: Products range from location tracking to automation; Duiven is at the simple end.

transition_in.carries_over: How products organize picking.
transition_in.introduces: How products differ by the building they serve, and where Duiven sits.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three facts about warehouse work shape every integration decision in the chapter: work has a release policy, the building has finite capacity, and its facts are physical, which makes the WMS the system of record for stock.

evidence.what: DeHoratius and Raman, Management Science 2008: 65% of nearly 370,000 stock records inaccurate across 37 stores of one retailer (older, pre-RFID).
evidence.shows: Records drift from the shelf without counting, so only the system that counts can be the record; a reminder, not a rate to assume.

transition_in.introduces: The third: its working day.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Cut-off, capacity and release policy belong in the data the delivery promise is computed from, and until they are, the promise is a sentence.

transition_in.carries_over: The three facts of the warehouse's day.
transition_in.introduces: Where they must go: the delivery promise.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A parcel and a wholesale pallet leave the same building through different processes, and a large retail customer expects a label on each logistics unit and an electronic message announcing what is on it.

transition_in.carries_over: The consumer parcel and its promise.
transition_in.introduces: The wholesale pallet and what retail customers expect.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The SSCC is the GS1 identifier of a logistics unit, the 18-digit number on the pallet label, and the despatch advice (DESADV, also called an ASN) tells the receiver what is coming pallet by pallet.

evidence.what: GS1 General Specifications, Release 26.0 (January 2026): the SSCC is 'the GS1 identifier for an individual logistics unit' and 'the only GS1 key that SHALL be used as the identifier of a logistic unit'.
evidence.shows: The standard fixes one identifier per pallet.

transition_in.carries_over: A label and a message.
transition_in.introduces: What each is.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Retailers enforce these rules: bol requires GS1 labels and the SSCC in DESADV messages, and Jumbo refuses deliveries without a matching DESADV and charges €70 per non-compliant message.

evidence.what: bol SSCC page (since 31 December 2021; n.d., accessed November 2026); Jumbo mechanized-DC guidelines (2025) and purchasing conditions (9 April 2026, €70 per message).
evidence.shows: Non-compliance is refused or charged.

transition_in.carries_over: The SSCC and the DESADV.
transition_in.introduces: Retailers that enforce them, with penalties.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Retail chargebacks come in two families, delivery performance (a logistics problem) and data and label compliance (an architecture problem), as Jumbo's delivery-performance penalty shows beside its message fee.

evidence.what: Jumbo purchasing conditions (€250 per order below 90% on time and in full on an order line).
evidence.shows: Delivery penalties are distinct from message penalties.

transition_in.carries_over: Jumbo's fee for a non-compliant message.
transition_in.introduces: Its separate penalty for late or incomplete deliveries, and the two families of chargebacks.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The DESADV must be generated from what the warehouse actually packed, never from the order, as Kestrel & Pine's €14,200 ASN Chargeback and Waypoint decision W6 show, with Bergzicht's April 2027 reorder as the first cycle under the new rule.

evidence.what: ASN Chargeback (Q3 2026): €14,200 deducted by Bergzicht because the DESADV came from the ERP's view of the order while the WMS packed something different; W6 moves SSCC generation to the WMS at pack time; Bergzicht's spring reorder (240 units, 18 SKUs, three pallets, delivered to Zwolle on 9 April 2027).
evidence.shows: Only pack time knows the pallet's SSCC and contents.

transition_in.carries_over: Data and label compliance as the architecture family of chargebacks.
transition_in.introduces: Where the message must be generated to avoid them.

sections.heading: The Choices: Who Runs the Warehouse Software
sections.controlling_idea: A merchant has four ways to get warehouse execution (an ERP module, a dedicated WMS, a 3PL or a marketplace fulfillment program), each fitting different conditions, and whichever it chooses the integration stays the same contract and the warehouse system must not become a second order system.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the contract is independent of who runs the warehouse software.

flow.rationale: The four options in rising order of how much the merchant hands over, then the shared-pool variant of the last, then what that stock is for the merchant (the paragraph the comparison table follows), then the recommendation that follows from the table.

transition_in.carries_over: The contract the warehouse system needs with the rest of the landscape.
transition_in.introduces: The choice of who runs the warehouse software.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A merchant has four realistic ways to get warehouse execution, and most use two at once.
The ERP's warehouse module is one system and one integration fewer and fits one building with modest volume and simple routes, but strains when waves, labor or several companies must be managed.

evidence.what: Odoo Inventory (n.d., accessed November 2026).
evidence.shows: A public example of an ERP warehouse module.

transition_in.carries_over: The four ways.
transition_in.introduces: The first: the ERP's module.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A dedicated WMS ranges from small cloud products to enterprise products with labor planning, automation and multiple sites, and should be chosen against the building's workflow and integration requirements.

evidence.what: Picqer (about 25 to 5,000+ orders daily); Manhattan, Blue Yonder, Infios (n.d., accessed November 2026).
evidence.shows: The two segments and their scale.

transition_in.carries_over: The ERP's module.
transition_in.introduces: The second: a dedicated WMS.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A 3PL runs the building on its own WMS and is integrated exactly like the merchant's own WMS, so it fits when volume, geography or season does not justify a building and fails when the merchant's process is the product.

transition_in.carries_over: Software the merchant runs.
transition_in.introduces: The third: a provider that runs the building.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A marketplace's fulfillment program stores and ships the seller's stock for fees per unit, order and storage period, delegating operations while making the seller dependent on that network's rules.

evidence.what: Amazon FBA (n.d.); Zalando ZFS (launched autumn 2017, 100+ partner brands by June 2019, older source); ZFS invoice structure updated 16 February 2026 (€0.15 peak surcharge per outbound order from 15 October to 31 January).
evidence.shows: Fees and dependence are documented.

transition_in.carries_over: A provider that runs one building for the merchant.
transition_in.introduces: The fourth: a marketplace's network.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Zalando's ZEOS extends the program to brands' other channels through a single shared stock pool, which is the availability problem run by the provider instead of the merchant.

evidence.what: Zalando: ZEOS announcement (October 2023), NEXT partnership (November 2024), letter to shareholders of 12 March 2026 (24 markets, 18 sales channels).
evidence.shows: A provider can run the shared stock pool.

transition_in.carries_over: The marketplace fulfillment program.
transition_in.introduces: Its extension to other channels.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For the merchant, marketplace-held stock is a location it can see but not count, a separate location with its own buffer fed by an inbound flow; Kestrel & Pine sends about 40% of its German marketplace units to such a program.

evidence.what: About 40% of Kestrel & Pine's German marketplace units go to the marketplace's program.
evidence.shows: The case applies to Kestrel & Pine.

evidence.what: Five rows (ERP module, small or mid-sized WMS, enterprise WMS, 3PL, marketplace program) by fits when, limits when and what the integration looks like.
evidence.shows: The integration is the same contract in every row except where the stock cannot be counted.

transition_in.carries_over: A provider-run stock pool.
transition_in.introduces: What that stock is in the merchant's own availability model.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Read across the table, the integration is the same contract in every row except that marketplace stock cannot be counted, so the author's recommendation follows the requirements, not the product (platform or ERP for one location and channel, a dedicated WMS for one building with several channels, an enterprise WMS or capable 3PL for several buildings or wholesale), always behind the same contract and never letting the warehouse system become a second order system, which is how Kestrel & Pine came to count orders three ways.

transition_in.carries_over: The four choices side by side.
transition_in.introduces: Which to choose when, and the one rule for all of them.

sections.heading: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits
sections.controlling_idea: Warehouse integration must grow with operational complexity through the four stages, and Kestrel & Pine bought an Omnichannel-stage WMS in 2023 but kept a Starting-stage connection.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that the integration, not the software, is what falls behind as a merchant grows.

transition_in.carries_over: Which execution choice fits which situation.
transition_in.introduces: How the setup and its warning signs change across the four scale stages.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Which execution setup fits changes as a merchant grows, and a table follows the typical setup, what becomes necessary and the warning signs through the four scale stages.

evidence.what: Four stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group) by typical setup, what becomes necessary and warning signs.
evidence.shows: Each stage adds a contract element: the handshake, stock events, a sized queue and reconciliation, one contract for every site.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Software can be bought, rented or outsourced, but integration still needs to match operational complexity, and Kestrel & Pine bought its WMS in 2023 while keeping an early-stage connection (orders pushed one by one, status pulled by the ERP, stock copied hourly).

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine's 2023 WMS with orders pushed one by one, status pulled by the ERP and stock copied hourly.
evidence.shows: The software reached stage 3 while the integration stayed at stage 1 or 2.

transition_in.carries_over: The stage table's setups and warning signs.
transition_in.introduces: Kestrel & Pine as a case of software and integration at different stages.

sections.heading: Warehouse Automation and Robotics
sections.controlling_idea: Automation and robots sit beneath the WMS and change how work is executed, not the need to confirm physical results: each automated task needs an identity, a confirmed outcome and a recovery path, and equipment downtime belongs in the delivery promise.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that adding automation keeps the chapter's contract (instructions with identity, confirmed results, capacity fed to the promise) one level down.

flow.rationale: Why automation is attractive and what it costs, then the four uses, then the software responsibilities and their documented division, then the task contract, then a hypothetical failure that tests it, then the advice to measure first: the contract only makes sense once the reader knows which layers send and confirm tasks.

transition_in.carries_over: The stage table, whose Group stage adds automation, and the contract the WMS keeps whatever runs it.
transition_in.introduces: The layers beneath the WMS in an automated warehouse, where the same contract applies one level down.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: As a warehouse grows it may add automation, and moving goods automatically can free pickers' walking time, but it adds coordination work: deciding which movement happens next, confirming that it happened and recovering when equipment stops.

The main uses of automation differ: mobile transport (autonomous mobile robots) moves containers, goods-to-person brings stock to a stationary picker, robotic picking grasps individual items and sortation routes items or parcels to their next lane.

evidence.what: Dematic's mobile-robot and robotic-picking pages (n.d., accessed November 2026).
evidence.shows: The four uses are documented separately by a vendor.

evidence.what: Figure 4: four uses of warehouse automation.
evidence.shows: Shows each use and that goods-to-person still leaves the item choice to a person.

transition_in.carries_over: Automation in general.
transition_in.introduces: Its four main uses.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Automated warehouses commonly divide the software into four responsibilities (WMS, warehouse execution system, warehouse control system and robot fleet management); the names describe jobs that products may combine.

evidence.what: WMS owns stock and tasks; WES releases and sequences work; WCS commands equipment; fleet management assigns robot tasks.
evidence.shows: Only the WMS owns stock records; the other layers execute.

transition_in.carries_over: The physical equipment.
transition_in.introduces: The software layers that direct it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Dematic's software overview and SAP's 2023 integration guide document this division, with warehouse orders becoming robot tasks and notifications returning to confirm the warehouse work.

evidence.what: Dematic software overview (n.d., accessed November 2026); SAP Warehouse Robotics, End-User Information for Integration via Fleet Management Systems (2023-12-20).
evidence.shows: Work flows down and confirmations flow back up in documented products.

evidence.what: Figure 5: the WMS, WES, WCS and fleet stack.
evidence.shows: The order system talks only to the WMS, the only layer that updates stock.

transition_in.carries_over: The four software responsibilities.
transition_in.introduces: Public documentation of the division and of confirmations flowing back.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author recommends keeping the order system connected to the WMS through fulfillment orders (the instruction to ship specified in the previous section) and requiring, inside the warehouse, an explicit contract for each automated task: a stable identity and instruction, a confirmed outcome from which the WMS updates stock, and recovery that queries the existing task before retrying.

evidence.what: SAP's guide on exception queues and physical checks before closing stalled tasks.
evidence.shows: Recovery by query and physical check is documented practice.

transition_in.carries_over: Work sent down and confirmations returned.
transition_in.introduces: What each automated task must carry for that to be safe.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: If Daniel later added robots, a robot that accepted a transfer, lost connectivity and delivered anyway would need the integration to recover that transfer's result rather than issue a new one, and the container reaching packing would still not prove the parcel shipped.

evidence.what: Hypothetical: a robot transfer at Duiven times out and is delivered anyway (labelled 'Suppose').
evidence.shows: A timeout leaves the outcome unknown; reissuing creates a second movement.

evidence.what: Figure 6: task T-4711 and its timeout story.
evidence.shows: Query the same task, then an exception queue for a physical check.

transition_in.carries_over: The task contract.
transition_in.introduces: A hypothetical Duiven failure that tests it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Before buying automation, measure where work waits, because faster transport helps only while packing and dispatch can absorb it, and feed queue age, equipment availability and reduced capacity into the delivery promise.

evidence.what: Figure 7: faster transport, same bottleneck.
evidence.shows: Faster transport moves the queue to packing; a stopped sorter removes dispatch capacity while stock still exists.

transition_in.carries_over: Automation's coordination risks.
transition_in.introduces: Whether it helps at all, and what it changes in the promise.

sections.heading: In Practice
sections.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine's own orders show its early-stage connection at work: Eva's late parcel and the Black Friday queue are one gap between the promise and the warehouse, closed by a queue, batches, a backlog monitor and a moving cut-off.

advances_thesis.how: Works the promise-versus-warehouse gap through two Kestrel & Pine cases and names the remedy.

flow.rationale: One order (Eva's) first, then the same gap at Black Friday scale, then its remedy: the evening reads as Eva's problem multiplied, so Eva comes first, and the remedy can only be named once the gap is seen at scale.

transition_in.carries_over: Automation as a hypothetical for Duiven, after Kestrel & Pine's stage-3 WMS behind an early-stage connection.
transition_in.introduces: Back at manual Duiven, Kestrel & Pine's own orders worked through that connection.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Eva's order, created in the WMS at 21:16 after the 21:00 final wave, is picked in the 06:30 wave on 14 April, confirmed at 08:40 and delivered on Thursday 15 April against a promise of Wednesday, because the promise was not computed from the warehouse.

evidence.what: Order #1072455: placed 21:14, in the WMS 21:16 (illustrative), 06:30 wave with about 180 other orders (illustrative), 1.1 kg box, confirmed 08:40 with tracking number and stock event, collected that evening, delivered 15 April; promised 14 April.
evidence.shows: The warehouse did nothing wrong; the promise ignored the cut-off.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Black Friday 2026 is the same gap at scale: 2,300 orders in the peak hour against an iPaaS flow, falling behind since the early afternoon, that created orders one at a time with several calls each and was throttled by the WMS vendor's rate limit, a four-hour backlog by 21:00 and roughly 8,000 orders that missed next-day delivery while the storefront promised it.

evidence.what: Peak hour 20:00 to 21:00: 2,300 orders (38 a minute); the iPaaS flow created orders one at a time with several API calls each and was throttled (illustrative mechanism); backlog four hours by 21:00; roughly 8,000 orders between 17:00 and midnight missed next-day delivery (assumption); Picqer publishes an API limit of about 500 requests per minute (n.d., accessed November 2026) as an example of a vendor rate limit.
evidence.shows: The feed, not the warehouse, was the limit.
evidence.source: Kestrel & Pine scenario ledger (_research/scenario-ledger.md), warehouse-and-fulfillment line

transition_in.carries_over: Eva's single order that missed its promise.
transition_in.introduces: The same gap for thousands of orders.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: What would have prevented it is not a faster warehouse but a queue allowed to grow without failing checkout, batched order creation within the rate limit, a monitor on the age of the oldest unprocessed order and a cut-off that moves with that age, all on Waypoint's list under W2 and W5.

evidence.what: Figure 8: the Queue That Waited and its cure.
evidence.shows: Before and after: a jammed feed versus a growing queue releasing batches with a backlog-age gauge.

transition_in.carries_over: The four-hour backlog and the broken promise.
transition_in.introduces: The four remedies.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong
sections.controlling_idea: Beyond the Black Friday queue, the warehouse interface fails in seven recognizable ways, each with a detection and a recovery that the contract makes possible.

advances_thesis.how: Shows each element of the contract by what happens without it.

flow.rationale: Failures of the instruction first (duplicates, late cancellations), then of what comes back (confirmations and the short picks behind partial ones, then stock events), then of shared identifiers, then of availability: the order the earlier sections built the contract in.

transition_in.carries_over: The remedies for the Black Friday queue.
transition_in.introduces: The other ways the warehouse interface fails.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Beyond the Black Friday queue, the warehouse interface fails in a small number of other recognizable ways, each with a detection and a recovery.
A retried instruction creates two pick lists and two jackets unless every message carries a fulfillment-order identity and the WMS creates idempotently, alerting instead of picking twice.

transition_in.carries_over: Failures with detections and recoveries.
transition_in.introduces: The first: duplicate fulfillment orders.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A cancellation made in the shop platform after the WMS accepted the order ships anyway unless the cancellation is a request with an answer the platform shows, so the order stays in progress and the item comes back as a return.

transition_in.carries_over: A duplicated instruction.
transition_in.introduces: An instruction withdrawn too late.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A shipment confirmation that is lost, or that marks a whole order fulfilled when only one of its parcels has left, leaves the shop platform, the WMS and the ERP telling different stories, as Kestrel & Pine's Three-Status Order shows; a per-shipment reconciliation detects it and a replay from the WMS repairs it.

evidence.what: Order #1052877 (December 2026): the fleece shipped first; the iPaaS flow, with no notion of a partial shipment, marked the whole order fulfilled on that first confirmation, so the platform showed Delivered, the WMS In picking while the socks waited, and the ERP, which invoiced only on 'order complete', Not invoiced for six days.
evidence.shows: A confirmation that does not arrive once per shipment makes three systems disagree.
evidence.source: consistency-issues.md items 2 and 14; Kestrel & Pine scenario ledger (_research/scenario-ledger.md)

transition_in.carries_over: Failures of the instruction.
transition_in.introduces: Failures of what comes back: the shipment confirmation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A short pick, where the record said one and the shelf has none, is recorded against the fulfillment order, which then ships partially or closes incomplete while the order system decides what to do with the line.

transition_in.carries_over: A confirmation that must report a partial shipment as partial.
transition_in.introduces: The commonest cause of a partial shipment: an empty location at pick time.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stock events that arrive out of order or not at all leave the available figure wrong until sequence numbers and a reconciliation catch them and the daily snapshot is reapplied.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine's May 2027 reconciliation (2.3% of active variants differing).
evidence.shows: Lost events produce measurable drift.

transition_in.carries_over: Failures of the shipment confirmation, including the short pick behind a partial one.
transition_in.introduces: The other message that comes back: stock events.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A SKU that differs between the shop platform and the WMS by a suffix, case or leading zero rejects or misroutes the fulfillment order until one identifier family is owned by the product system and published to both.

evidence.what: Shopify: SKU strings are case-sensitive (n.d., accessed November 2026).
evidence.shows: A difference of case alone breaks the match.

transition_in.carries_over: Stock figures that drift between the warehouse and its copies.
transition_in.introduces: A failure in the identifiers both sides share.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A WMS outage on a peak evening is detected by the age of the oldest queued order and recovered with the same remedies as the Black Friday queue: queue rather than fail checkout, release in batches within the rate limit, move the cut-off while the backlog is old.

transition_in.carries_over: Failures of single messages and identifiers.
transition_in.introduces: The failure of the whole warehouse system.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The missing jacket, Eva's Wednesday promise and the Black Friday queue look like a stock error, a storefront sentence and an integration fault; read together they are one failure, a promise made from a copy or a sentence instead of from the warehouse's own facts, and the chapter's contract (a keyed fulfillment order with an answer, one writer of on hand, confirmations from what was packed, a cut-off read from the queue) is the one remedy for all three.
conclusion.so_what: A merchant can write the fulfillment-order contract, name the one writer of on-hand stock and feed the cut-off and backlog to the promise before it buys a WMS, a 3PL or robots; Kestrel & Pine's Black Friday remedy was a queue, batches, a monitor and a moving cut-off, not a faster warehouse.

callback.to: The opening's picker who finds no jacket for a paid order.
callback.how: The first paragraph of the conclusion names the warehouse fact each failure ignored and what the warehouse must receive and report so the shop's promise holds.

takeaway.content: Write the fulfillment-order contract with its key and its answer, name the one writer of on-hand stock, feed the cut-off and backlog to the delivery promise, and take the ten questions to your own warehouse.

hand_off.carries_over: The parcel packed and confirmed at Duiven, and the cut-off, capacity and backlog that the storefront's promise ignored.
hand_off.introduces: The carrier's part: labels, manifests and tracking events, and a delivery promise computed from the warehouse's facts and the carrier's transit time.

transition_in.carries_over: The ways the warehouse interface fails and how each is detected and recovered.
transition_in.introduces: The chapter's answer set against its opening, then what holds across the chapter, sorted by how settled it is.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The opening's missing jacket, Eva's day-late parcel and the Black Friday queue are one failure: a promise made from a sentence or a copy instead of from the warehouse's own facts; a fulfillment order with a key and an answer, one writer of on-hand stock, confirmations built from what was packed and a cut-off read from the queue let the shop promise only what the warehouse can do.

evidence.what: The opening's picker who finds no jacket, set against the chapter's contract.
evidence.shows: The reader can now say which warehouse fact each of the three failures ignored.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Established: warehouses have finite capacity and carrier deadlines, documented fulfillment models have an acceptance step, stock records drift without counting, and large retail customers require SSCC-labelled units announced by a matching DESADV.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapter's answer in one paragraph.
transition_in.introduces: The points it rests on, starting with what the sources establish.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Depends on context: an ERP module suits a simple building, outsourcing suits seasonal or regional volume, periodic sync works while its lag is shorter than a sell-out, and DESADV generation from packing matters only for merchants with retail customers.

transition_in.carries_over: What is established.
transition_in.introduces: What changes with the merchant's situation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's synthesis: keep fulfillment instructions and confirmed results stable when changing vendors or adding robots, and compute delivery promises from remaining capacity, queues and carrier deadlines.

transition_in.carries_over: What is established and what depends on context.
transition_in.introduces: The author's own judgement, labelled as such.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ten questions let the reader check, in their own company, what the warehouse receives, the acceptance step, timeout recovery, who writes on hand, how stock changes travel, reconciliation, the cut-off, the order feed's capacity, wholesale labels and the outage plan.

transition_in.carries_over: The take-aways.
transition_in.introduces: Questions that apply them to the reader's own company.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: With Eva's parcel packed and confirmed at Duiven, the carrier takes over, and the next chapter follows carrier selection, labels and tracking and builds a delivery promise from the warehouse's cut-off, capacity and backlog that the storefront's sentence ignored.

transition_in.carries_over: The questions about the reader's own warehouse.
transition_in.introduces: The packed parcel handed to the carrier and the promise the next chapter computes.

non_goals.topic: Robot selection, mechanical design, motion planning and machinery safety engineering; the automation section covers integration responsibilities and operational consequences.
Available-to-promise, reservations, allocation, safety stock and the availability service as such; this chapter uses on hand, committed and available only to say what the warehouse writes.
The order state machine, order splits, sourcing and routing, and the OMS as a product.

EDI messages, Peppol, mapping and partner onboarding; this chapter decides only where the SSCC and the DESADV are generated.
Peak planning, queues and backpressure in general; the chapter shows the Black Friday queue from the warehouse's side only.
